body:
# Independent audit: exponentially moving convex hinge

Audited source:
`candidate 06f3c3316a88c7ba`.


separator, its pointwise O(lambda_j) remainder, exponential floor, and
the actual joint geometric group/cap kernels. The full new source and
its cap-kernel dependency were read. This audit proves no lower bound
on the remaining captured inverse-density term.

## 1. Convexity and actual paths

The function L_j is a finite minimum of affine functions, so
-exp(R/lambda_j)L_j is finite convex on the full ambient space. Adding
the finite convex f and taking a positive part preserves convexity.
Multiplication by the nonnegative normal scalar psi preserves it for
each fixed normal. Thus the new field belongs to the actual cone; it
is not the product of two physical convex functions.

At each fixed j the exponential coefficient is finite. On compact
sets the field is continuous and bounded, even though its derivative
or its values farther outside the current body can be very large.
For t>=0 each normal-cut inequality has a convex left side, so its
intersection defines a convex fiber. Because the field is nonnegative,
the new fiber lies in the old one. A current fixed-j inball survives
when t is sufficiently small, by a bound on the field on that inball
and compact normal sphere. No uniform lower bound for this permitted
time is needed by the local separator.

For an anchored convex combination of fiber points, convexity of the
field bounds its new left side by the corresponding average of the
input left sides. Original support-function compatibility then puts
the combination in the target fiber. This preserves the canonical
hull's exact sampled fibers and its complete integer base, as in the
audited full-cone construction. Dependence of the field on the current
L_j is harmless: it is held fixed as a test at that selected minimum.

## 2. The support restriction validates the rescaling

Write p_j=[f-exp(R/lambda_j)L_j]_+ and let F bound f on the common
compact physical support. On {p_j>0},

    L_j<F exp(-R/lambda_j),
    r_j>R-lambda_j log F>=R/2

for all sufficiently large j. Here L_j<1, so ell_j,+ =-log L_j exactly.
Consequently the identity

    (1/lambda_j) d eta_j = (1/r_j) d B_j

is valid on the support of p_j, where B_j=ell_j,+ eta_j with its
joint rate coordinate. One may define p_j/r_j to be zero off that
support; no division by zero occurs.

Dividing the exact physical inequality by lambda_j gives exactly

    integral psi p_j/r_j d A_j
       -beta_j integral psi p_j/r_j d B_j
       +integral psi p_j d B_j
       +remainder <=0.

The term r_j in Xi_j cancels the reciprocal rate in the third term.
The pointwise bound |R_j|<=C lambda_j gives the remainder estimate

    |remainder|<=C integral psi p_j d eta_j
       <=C lambda_j (2F/R)||psi||_infinity B_j(total),

which tends to zero. Uniformly bounded log-measure mass, not any
global bound for eta_j/lambda_j, is the exact needed hypothesis.

## 3. Moving-threshold limit and both endpoint conventions

On the retained log-measure support, p_j can be expressed as
[f-exp((R-r)/lambda_j)]_+. Away from an arbitrarily small strip about
r=R, this converges uniformly to f 1_(r>R). Its quotient by r is
uniformly bounded by 2F/R on its support. At a threshold having zero
limiting log-measure mass, the strip is removable: Portmanteau bounds
its limsup mass by a closed strip's limiting mass, which decreases
to zero. The cap-load measure is dominated by the same log measure,
so the same argument works for it simultaneously.

The ordinary parts at rate zero cannot contribute, because the test
support is eventually in r>=R/2. Bounded total test integrals also
justify replacing beta_j by beta. Thus the source's upper-tail
inequality (5) follows with precisely its reciprocal rate and its
unweighted reserve term.

Continuity thresholds decreasing to R yield the open tail by monotone
convergence. Those increasing to R yield the closed tail by continuity
from above of finite measures, with all rates bounded below by a
positive number. Each term is nonnegative; passing these terms
separately preserves the inequality. The source correctly does not
subtract the open and closed inequalities to assert an atom inequality.
At R=beta>0, the support bound leaves only the top atom, so direct
cancellation in the closed-tail inequality does imply that the
cap-load defect at rate beta vanishes.

The exact three-atom separation check is correct. The old signed
budget is (1/10)(delta_(1/5)-2delta_(2/5)+delta_(3/5)), nonnegative
against all convex functions. Its reciprocal-rate integral over a
tail retaining only the last two atoms is -1/2+1/6=-1/3. Thus the new
test is not obtained merely by choosing another old convex rate test.
The source limits this example to separation of measure restrictions,
without claiming an actual selected-body realization.

## 4. Canonical cap densities and positivity at every positive rate

The dependency supplies actual joint finite exterior, section, and
inverse measures with

    N_e=K mu_e,
    N_e,H=K(alpha_e,H+kappa_H s_e,H).

For each positive R, the signed weighted tail defining v_e,H(R) has
finite total variation, since 1/r is bounded above there and the
joint cap/section measures are finite. It is right-continuous in total
variation on positive rate intervals. The kernel identity says it
equals a positive inverse-density measure for almost every rate.
Taking a decreasing sequence of such rates to any specified R proves
positivity of its canonical right limit. Left limits, using closed
tails, are positive by the same argument. The finite joint cap-law
hypotheses permit the identical reasoning after cap-law integration.

A normal test isolating -e among the finite defect normal directions
is genuinely admissible. It does not select individual fibers, contact
rows, or a subcollection of groups sharing that direction. The full
cap law is retained. Outside the positive-parallel section class,
kappa_H s_e,H is zero or nonpositive, so the exterior reciprocal tail
dominates the actual inverse tail as a physical measure. Inside-class
exterior terms are nonnegative and may be discarded. This proves the
source's noninside comparison without deleting a positive section
correction or replacing a selector by a halfspace indicator.

## 5. Exact inverse-rate conversion

For t>R, the contribution of a surface atom of rate t to

    R v_e(R)+integral_R^infinity v_e(s) ds

is R/t+(t-R)/t=1. Positive-measure Tonelli therefore proves the exact
physical-measure identity for mu_e((R,infinity)). Substituting it into
the hinge inequality and then using the noninside comparison gives
the asserted pointwise positive inverse-rate payment with coefficient
R and no numerical loss.

Replacing v_e(R) by its left limit adds exactly the surface atom at R
divided by R. Multiplying by R restores that atom; the Lebesgue
integral term is unchanged. This proves the closed-tail version and
accounts for all endpoint mass. The derivation only tests the physical
measures by the originally admissible nonnegative convex f.

For a single physical point and one surface rate T, v_e is constant
on (0,T). The reserve is R+(T-R)=T times this density. A strictly
capturing noninside sublaw of weight p therefore gives p+T<=beta,
matching the prior atomic calibration. Multiple rates retain the new
canonical pointwise constraint.

## 6. Scope and necessary inherited assumptions

The moving field is valid only because the selected minimum has one
exact separator for the full normal-dependent convex cone. A separator
proved merely for a fixed bounded family of fields would not suffice.
Likewise the divided remainder needs the pointwise O(lambda_j) bound,
not just an unscaled weak vanishing statement. Both are explicitly
included in the source.

The canonical tail conversion inherits finiteness and joint measurability
of cap/section defects from the cited actual cap-flux theorem. It does
not establish those properties for arbitrary separately chosen limiting
records. With those dependencies retained, no repair is required.
There remains no proved universal lower bound on the noninside term,
and neither its positivity nor this audit supplies the OC constant.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
